kurals.tamil:
வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும்
துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaivaliyum thanvaliyum maatraan valiyum
Thunaivaliyum thookkich cheyal.
kurals.meaning: Before acting, weigh four strengths against one another: the strength the task demands, your own strength, your opponent’s strength, and the strength of the allies who will stand with each side.
kurals.elementary: Before you start something big, stop and measure four things: how hard the job is, how strong you are, how strong the other side is, and who will help each of you. Only after weighing all four should you decide to go ahead.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a four-part audit: vinai-vali (the strength the undertaking requires), tan-vali (one’s own strength), maatraan-vali (the adversary’s) and thunai-vali (the strength of allies, which Parimelazhagar reads as the allies of both parties). The verb thookki, ‘weighing as on a balance’, governs all four terms, so action (seyal) is justified only by comparison. Assessing yourself alone is not enough. This is the centre of the Kural’s political realism, and it closely parallels Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, whose ninth book opens with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness before any campaign. Prudence here is not timidity. It is what makes effective action possible.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra opens its book on the conqueror’s campaigns with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness. There the would-be invader compares his own powers with the enemy’s: the power of counsel, the power of treasury and army, and the power of energy and valour. He marches only when that comparison favours him.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya makes assessment of relative strength a formal step that must come before any war. The king has to know both his own resources and the enemy’s, and has to account for place and season too.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s fourfold weighing. Valluvar even adds allies (thunai-vali) as a separate item on the scale.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical doctrine, even down to the chapter heading about ‘knowledge of power’. Paraphrased; the Shamasastry wording could not be re-checked verbatim this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses a king comparing troop numbers to illustrate counting the cost before committing. A king who finds himself outmatched negotiates instead of fighting.
christianity.tie_back: It pairs one’s own strength against the opponent’s before acting, which is the core of the Kural’s weighing. The Kural adds the task’s strength and allies’ strength as further items.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match on comparing one’s own strength with the enemy’s. In Luke the image serves a lesson about discipleship, while in the Kural it is literal statecraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “Now, Allah has lightened [the hardship] for you, and He knows that among you is weakness. So if there are from you one hundred [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: The verse sets a realistic ratio of strength for the believers’ military obligation. It takes their actual weakness into account and does not demand the impossible.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a sober calculation of one’s own force against the enemy’s as the basis for deciding whether to fight.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the explicit strength-ratio reasoning. The Qur’anic frame is divine permission and steadfastness rather than purely prudential assessment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb insists that war, of all undertakings, must be entered only after deliberation and sound advice.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s demand that action follow careful weighing, though the four strengths are not spelled out.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same principle of deliberating before war, but more general. It has no explicit inventory of strengths.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajātasattu, planning to attack the Vajjians, sends his minister Vassakāra to ask the Buddha what will happen. The Buddha asks Ānanda whether the Vajjians still keep seven conditions of welfare, including meeting often, acting in concord and honouring their elders. He concludes that while they keep them, they can be expected to prosper and not decline.
buddhism.explanation: The episode is in effect an assessment of the opponent’s real strength. The minister leaves understanding that the Vajjians cannot be conquered by force while they remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: It dramatises maatraan-vali, knowing the enemy’s actual strength before attacking, which is one of the Kural’s four weights.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel for assessing an opponent. The Buddha’s purpose is to teach the conditions of communal welfare, not military strategy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the Achaeans march on Troy, old Nestor advises Agamemnon to array the army by tribes and clans so that each group supports its own. That way he will learn which chiefs and men are brave and which are cowards, and whether any failure comes from heaven or from human weakness.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor proposes organising the army so that its real strength, including the reliability of allies and contingents, becomes visible before the decisive fight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s concern with knowing one’s own strength and one’s allies’ strength (thunai-vali) before acting.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial match covering assessment of one’s own and allied forces. It does not weigh the enemy or the task.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu holds that victory follows from accurate knowledge of both one’s own condition and the enemy’s. Ignorance of either brings defeat.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the closest single-sentence analogue to the Kural’s instruction to weigh one’s own and the opponent’s strength before acting.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III.18 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on self and enemy. The Kural adds the task’s demands and allied strength.

kurals.tamil:
ஒல்வ தறிவது அறிந்ததன் கண்தங்கிச்
செல்வார்க்குச் செல்லாதது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Olvadhu arivadhu arindhadhan kan thangich
Chelvaarkkuch chellaadhadhu il.
kurals.meaning: Nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do, learn what the task requires, and then keep steadily at it as they go forward.
kurals.elementary: If you know what you’re able to do, learn everything you need for it, and then stick with it without giving up, there’s nothing you can’t reach.
kurals.university: This couplet turns the caution of 471 into confidence. It has three stages: olvadhu (discerning what is within one’s power), arivadhu (acquiring the knowledge the task needs) and thangi (settling into the work with steady application). The conclusion, chellaadhadhu il (‘there is nothing that will not go’ for such people), is not a claim to unlimited power. It is conditional: success without limit is promised only inside the field that honest self-assessment has marked out. Knowing your limits is exactly what lets you be effective within them. The verse also defends Valluvar’s realism against the charge of defeatism, since measuring your strength is meant to lead to action, not to paralysis.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that it is better to perform one’s own duty (svadharma), even imperfectly, than another’s duty well. Work suited to one’s own nature does not bring sin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita directs each person to the field of action that fits their own nature and capacity, rather than an ambitious role that belongs to someone else.
hinduism.tie_back: This resembles the Kural’s olvadhu, knowing what is truly one’s own to accomplish, as the ground on which steady effort succeeds.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of acting within one’s own nature and capacity. The Gita’s svadharma is also a matter of social and religious duty, while the Kural’s concern is practical capability. Paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, each servant is entrusted in proportion to his ability. Those who work faithfully with what they have are rewarded.
christianity.tie_back: Capacity is measured first and diligence follows, much like the Kural’s sequence of knowing what one can do and then persisting in it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel on responsibility matched to ability. The parable is eschatological, and the ability is assessed by the master rather than by the servant himself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commends deeds done within one’s capacity and kept up steadily, over bursts of effort that cannot be sustained.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s pairing of realistic scope (olvadhu) with steady perseverance (thangi) as the way to reach one’s aim.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on sustainable effort within capacity. The hadith concerns devotional acts, not worldly undertakings.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses assures Israel that the commandment is neither too hard nor too far off. It lies within their reach, so they can carry it out.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it frames a task correctly understood as within one’s capacity, and therefore as achievable.
judaism._accuracy_note: Weaker match. The text reassures that the Torah is within reach but has no teaching on self-assessment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Soṇa, exhausted by excessive striving, thinks of giving up. The Buddha reminds him that a lute plays well only when its strings are neither too taut nor too slack. In the same way, over-aroused persistence leads to restlessness and slack persistence to laziness, so Soṇa should find the right pitch of effort and then pursue his practice. Soṇa does so and attains arahantship.
buddhism.explanation: The lute simile teaches that attainment comes from effort tuned to one’s real capacity and then kept up. Neither strain nor laxity works.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s formula of knowing what one can do and then persisting in it. The result is also the same: the goal Soṇa despaired of turns out to be reachable.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel: measured capacity plus sustained effort leads to success. Paraphrased from the Thanissaro translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops’ cave, Odysseus is about to stab the sleeping Polyphemus. He stops when he realises that he and his men could never move the boulder blocking the entrance. Having recognised what is and is not within their power, he devises a plan that fits it, blinding the giant and escaping under the sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus succeeds because he first identifies the limit of his strength and then pursues only a plan that works within it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that knowing what is possible is what makes success possible.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative illustration of assessing capacity and then succeeding within it. It is a single episode, not a stated principle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus opens his Handbook by dividing all things into those within our power (judgement, impulse, desire, aversion) and those not within our power (body, property, reputation, office). He holds that someone who attends only to what is within their power cannot be thwarted.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, correctly identifying the sphere of one’s real power is the precondition of an unhindered life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises that nothing can stop those who understand where their power lies and act inside it. The Stoic version turns inward, while Valluvar’s looks outward to practical tasks.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shared logic of success within a correctly known sphere of power. Epictetus limits that sphere to the inner life, while the Kural means worldly capability.

kurals.tamil:
உடைத்தம் வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி
இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Udaiththam valiyariyaar ookkaththin ookki
Idaikkan murindhaar palar.
kurals.meaning: Many who did not know the true measure of their own strength, and plunged into an undertaking on enthusiasm alone, have broken down midway.
kurals.elementary: Lots of people get very excited and jump into something big without checking whether they’re strong enough. Halfway through they run out of strength, and it all falls apart.
kurals.university: Udaiththam vali, ‘the strength they themselves possess’, is exactly what these people fail to know. Ookkam (zeal, drive) is praised elsewhere in the Kural, with a whole chapter on it (ch. 60, Ookkam Udaimai), so Valluvar is not condemning enthusiasm itself. He condemns enthusiasm cut loose from measurement. The verb murindhaar (‘they snapped’) suggests a branch or axle giving way under strain and looks ahead to the cart-axle image of 475. Palar (‘many’) gives the verse an empirical, historical tone: this is not a hypothetical but a pattern seen across many careers and kingdoms.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita calls an action tamasic (of the mode of ignorance) when it is undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one’s own ability.
hinduism.explanation: Among the marks of deluded action, Krishna names disregard of one’s own capacity (pauruṣam anavekṣya).
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s diagnosis in doctrinal form: action begun without knowing one’s strength belongs to delusion and ends badly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The Sanskrit pauruṣam anavekṣya directly names disregard of one’s own capacity. Paraphrased, because translations of the verse vary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a builder who starts without reckoning his resources and is left with an unfinished tower and public ridicule.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Began to build, and was not able to finish’ closely matches the Kural’s idaikkan murindhaar, ‘broke down midway’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: failing to measure capacity leads to collapse midway. Luke applies it to the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that religion is easy, and that whoever overburdens himself in it will be overpowered and unable to continue. He advised believers to avoid extremes, to aim at what is right and come close to it, and to take heart.
islam.explanation: The hadith warns that zeal which ignores one’s real capacity cannot be sustained, and the zealous person gives up.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s picture of zeal without self-knowledge collapsing before it reaches the end.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on overextension leading to abandonment. The domain is religious practice. Paraphrased from the Muhsin Khan translation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes warns against eagerly undertaking obligations one cannot fulfil. It is wiser not to begin than to begin and fail.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns commitments made in enthusiasm without regard to capacity, which end unfinished.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel on unfulfilled commitments. It concerns vows specifically, not undertakings in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Before his awakening, the Bodhisatta pushed ascetic practice to the extreme, holding his breath and reducing food until his body wasted and he was near death. He found that these austerities did not lead to awakening, recalled a calmer state of absorption from his childhood, and took up the middle way.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s own story is one of overreaching zeal that nearly destroyed him partway along the path, until he adopted a practice suited to what a human body and mind can bear.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s warning that fervour beyond one’s real strength breaks down before reaching the goal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel of zeal outrunning capacity. The Buddha’s point is that extreme asceticism is futile, not only that it exhausts.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begs his father Helios to let him drive the chariot of the Sun. Helios warns him that not even Zeus could control those horses, but Phaethon insists. Partway across the sky he loses control, the horses bolt and scorch the earth, and Zeus strikes him down with a thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaethon’s eagerness overrides his father’s warning about the limits of his strength, and he fails in mid-course.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a mythic version of the Kural: zeal without knowing one’s strength, then collapse midway.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match: overconfident zeal and breakdown partway through the undertaking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus continues that someone who does not do this will begin eagerly, without thinking of the consequences, and then give up in disgrace when difficulties appear. He adds: consider first what the matter is and what your own nature can bear.
philosophy.tie_back: It is almost a commentary on the Kural: eager starts without self-assessment end in shameful abandonment midway.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one. Only the opening sentence is quoted; the rest is paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
அமைந்தாங் கொழுகான் அளவறியான் தன்னை
வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Amaindhaangu ozhugaan alavariyaan thannai
Viyandhaan viraindhu kedum.
kurals.meaning: One who does not act in harmony with others, does not know the measure of his own strength, and admires himself, will quickly come to ruin.
kurals.elementary: Someone who won’t get along with others, doesn’t know how strong they really are, and keeps bragging about how great they are will fall very fast.
kurals.university: Three faults are linked here. The first is failing to fit one’s conduct to others (amaindhaangu ozhugaan, which commentators read as refusing to accommodate those around one, especially more powerful neighbours). The second is ignorance of one’s own measure (alavu ariyaan). The third is self-admiration (thannai viyandhaan). The first two are errors of judgement, and the third is the emotional state that keeps them going, because the self-admirer stops checking. Viraindhu (‘swiftly’) matters: pride does not merely lead to ruin eventually, it speeds it up.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Confident in his army and his own prowess, Duryodhana rejects Krishna’s peace embassy and every counsel of Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and his own parents. He refuses to give the Pandavas even five villages, and the war that follows destroys him and his house.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana will not accommodate others, misjudges his real strength, and is swollen with self-regard, the three faults the Kural lists.
hinduism.tie_back: His swift ruin at Kurukshetra illustrates the Kural’s viraindhu kedum.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavad-yana sections; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match for all three faults. The war’s causes in the epic are also presented as fated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns against inflated self-estimation and calls for a sober judgement of oneself according to the measure actually given.
christianity.tie_back: It addresses the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: not knowing one’s measure, and thinking too highly of oneself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on sober self-measurement and against self-admiration. Paul’s ‘measure’ is spiritual gifting, not worldly power.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.”
islam.explanation: Luqman’s counsel to his son forbids arrogance toward people and conceited self-display.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s pairing of failing to get along with others and self-admiration. The Kural adds the practical consequence of swift ruin.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on arrogance and self-delusion. The Qur’an frames the result as divine disfavour rather than prudential ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb holds that pride is the prelude to collapse.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the same causal chain as the Kural’s thannai viyandhaan … kedum: self-exaltation leading to ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on pride leading to ruin. It does not mention knowing one’s measure or accommodating others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is called a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada treats inflated self-assessment as the deepest form of folly.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: not knowing one’s real measure and admiring oneself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on self-overestimation. It says nothing directly about swift ruin.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a gifted weaver, boasts that her skill surpasses Athena’s and refuses to admit any debt to the goddess. She rejects Athena’s warning, delivered in the guise of an old woman, and challenges her to a contest. Enraged, Athena destroys her work, and Arachne is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arachne’s self-admiration and refusal to accept advice bring swift ruin, even though her skill is real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s three faults: refusing to accommodate, misjudging one’s standing, and admiring oneself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on boastful self-regard leading to rapid downfall. The contest is against a god, which gives it a religious dimension of hubris.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After questioning a man reputed to be wise, Socrates concludes that he himself is wiser in one small way: neither of them knows anything fine and good, but the other man thinks he knows when he does not, while Socrates does not think he knows.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates makes accurate knowledge of one’s own limits the beginning of wisdom and exposes self-admiration as ignorance.
philosophy.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s alavu ariyaan and thannai viyandhaan: self-flattery comes from not knowing one’s own measure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on self-knowledge against self-regard. The domain is intellectual, not practical power, and ruin is not the point.

kurals.tamil:
பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் அப்பண்டஞ்
சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Peelipey saakaadum achchirum appandanj
Chaala miguththup peyin.
kurals.meaning: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers will have its axle break if the load is piled on beyond measure.
kurals.elementary: A peacock feather weighs almost nothing. But if you pile far too many onto a cart, even feathers will snap its axle. Lots of small things can add up to too much.
kurals.university: This is one of the Kural’s most famous images. The peacock feather (peeli) is the lightest of loads and the cart (saakaadu) a sturdy vehicle, yet when it is loaded chaala miguththu (‘in great excess’), the axle (achchu) breaks. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to kings: even weak enemies can overwhelm a strong ruler if they combine, so a king should not provoke many small foes at once. A broader reading applies it to any capacity. No strength is infinite, and sheer quantity can turn trifles into a fatal burden. The image anticipates the later proverb of the straw that breaks the camel’s back.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is regulated in his habits of eating, sleeping, recreation and work can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: The verse before it warns that yoga is not for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. The body has a measure that excess breaks.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats capacity as having a limit that must not be overloaded, even with ordinary, harmless things.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of measure against excess. It does not have the Kural’s specific point about small loads accumulating.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of wineskins that burst when strained beyond what they can hold.
christianity.tie_back: As with the Kural’s axle, a container or carrier fails when made to bear more than its capacity.
christianity._accuracy_note: The image of breaking under excess load is shared. Jesus’ point is about new teaching and old forms, not measuring strength.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity. … Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear.”
islam.explanation: The verse affirms that every soul has a limit of capacity and prays not to be loaded beyond it.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s picture of a burden that must stay within what the bearer can carry.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the principle of burden against capacity. It has no image of light things accumulating, and the frame is theological.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud repeatedly uses the principle ‘tafasta merubah lo tafasta’: if you grasp too much, you have not grasped anything; if you grasp a little, you have grasped it.
judaism.explanation: The sages use this maxim to choose the smaller of two possible measures, reasoning that overreaching loses everything.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that taking on more than can be held leads to losing it all.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 4b (also Yoma 80a, Chagigah 17a)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good proverbial parallel on overload. In context it is a legal-hermeneutic rule. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not think lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that small things, each negligible, accumulate until the vessel is full.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s insight that light items (drops, feathers) become decisive in quantity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared logic of small things accumulating. It is about moral karma rather than the limits of power.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a donkey heavily loaded begs the unburdened horse to take a share. The horse refuses, the donkey collapses and dies under the load, and the master then puts the whole burden, and the donkey’s hide, on the horse.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a carrier failing when loaded beyond its strength, and the burden then falling on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the same picture as the Kural’s overloaded cart: a bearer breaks when the load exceeds its capacity.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Horse and the Ass’ (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image parallel. Aesop’s moral is about mutual help rather than self-knowledge, and fable is not strictly myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that both excessive and deficient exercise destroy bodily strength, and that too much or too little food or drink destroys health, while the right amount produces, increases and preserves them. The virtues, he argues, are destroyed by excess and deficiency in the same way.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that even good and necessary things become destructive past their proper measure.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the philosophical form of the Kural’s point that excess of even a light thing breaks what bears it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.2, 1104a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on excess destroying strength. Paraphrased from Ross.

kurals.tamil:
நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார் அஃதிறந் தூக்கின்
உயிர்க்கிறுதி ஆகி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nunikkombar erinaar ahdhirandhu ookkin
Uyirkkirudhi aagi vidum.
kurals.meaning: Those who have climbed to the very tip of a branch will lose their lives if they try to climb beyond it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine climbing a tree right out to the thinnest tip of a branch. If you try to go even further, the branch breaks and you fall. You need to know when you’ve gone as high as you safely can.
kurals.university: Nunikkombar, the thin end of a branch, marks the exact limit of what one’s strength, and the support one relies on, can bear. Commentators apply it to a ruler who has already stretched his power as far as it will go: any further push (ahdhu irandhu ookkin, ‘if he strives beyond it’) becomes fatal. The verse pairs with 475. There an external load exceeds capacity; here one’s own ambition exceeds the support beneath. The image is precise: the danger is greatest exactly when one is highest.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Triśaṅku wants to ascend to heaven in his own body. Refused by his guru Vasiṣṭha and cursed by Vasiṣṭha’s sons, he turns to Viśvāmitra, whose ascetic power lifts him up. The gods throw him back down, and he is left suspended head-down in a heaven of his own between earth and the gods’ realm.
hinduism.explanation: Triśaṅku has already reached the height of a king’s station and tries to climb beyond the limit set for mortals. He ends suspended, neither risen nor safe.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a mythic version of trying to climb past the branch-tip.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good image of overreaching one’s limit. Triśaṅku does not die, and Viśvāmitra’s power complicates the moral.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.”
christianity.explanation: Set on the pinnacle of the Temple and urged to throw himself down trusting in rescue, Jesus refuses to go beyond the safe limit on the strength of presumption.
christianity.tie_back: Standing at the highest point, he declines to overreach, which is the restraint the Kural urges on the climber at the branch-tip.
christianity._accuracy_note: Loose parallel. The height image and refusal to overreach fit, but the point is about presumption toward God, not the limits of one’s strength.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds human beings of the fixed limits of their stature and strength against pride that imagines no ceiling.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a height beyond which human striving cannot go.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of a natural limit to human reach. It warns against arrogance rather than describing a fatal fall.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.”
judaism.explanation: The builders of Babel try to push human achievement past its proper limit. Their project is halted and they are scattered.
judaism.tie_back: It is a biblical form of the Kural’s climbing past the tip: reaching for more than the limit allows ends in collapse.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good image of overreaching height. The result is dispersion, not death, and the frame is divine judgement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, already a respected monk with psychic powers and the patronage of Prince Ajātasattu, asks to take over leadership of the Saṅgha from the Buddha. When refused, he plots against the Buddha’s life and splits the order. The tradition records that he fell into ruin.
buddhism.explanation: Having reached a high position, Devadatta reaches beyond it and destroys himself.
buddhism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that striving past the limit one has already reached is fatal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate parallel of ambition overreaching a high position. Devadatta’s fault is mainly malice, not misjudged strength.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus makes wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus and warns him to fly a middle course, neither too low near the sea nor too high near the sun. Icarus, thrilled by flight, soars upward. The sun softens the wax, the feathers fall away, and he plunges into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus climbs past the height his means can bear and dies for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the closest mythic parallel to the Kural’s climber who goes beyond the branch-tip.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a known limit of height, ambition past it, fatal fall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Artabanus warns Xerxes against invading Greece. He points out that the god strikes the tallest creatures, buildings and trees with his thunderbolt, and brings low whatever towers above the rest.
philosophy.explanation: Herodotus’ wise adviser argues that greatness pushed further exposes one to catastrophe.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s insight that danger is greatest at the highest point and that pressing further brings destruction.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong parallel, with even the tree image. Herodotus attributes the fall to divine jealousy, while the Kural’s cause is physical and prudential. Paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள்
போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu eega adhuporul
Potri vazhangu neri.
kurals.meaning: Give in the right way, knowing the measure of your means. That is the way to preserve your wealth while still giving it.
kurals.elementary: Being generous is good, but give in a way that fits what you actually have. That way you can keep helping people and still keep your household going.
kurals.university: Here the chapter turns from military to economic power, since for Valluvar wealth is also a form of vali. Aatrin means ‘in the proper way’, or in some readings ‘according to one’s capacity’. Alavu arindhu means knowing the measure of one’s wealth. The couplet reconciles two duties that could conflict: potri (preserving) and vazhangu (distributing). Measured giving is not stinginess. It is the method (neri) that makes generosity sustainable. Some web editions print aravarindhu here, but the standard Parimelazhagar text and most editions read alavarindhu, ‘knowing the measure’, which fits the chapter’s theme.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s parting charge to graduating students, the teacher lays down how gifts are to be given: with faith, not without faith; śriyā deyam (in keeping with one’s prosperity); with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad regulates the manner and proportion of giving, not only the act.
hinduism.tie_back: If śriyā deyam is read as ‘give in keeping with one’s means’, it parallels the Kural’s alavu arindhu eega.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Depends on interpretation: śriyā deyam is also rendered ‘give in plenty’ or ‘give with grace’. Paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not. For I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Corinthians that a gift is measured by what the giver has, and that generosity is not meant to relieve others by crushing the giver.
christianity.tie_back: This is very close to the Kural’s instruction to give knowing one’s measure, so that giving and preserving go together.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on giving in proportion to means without self-ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not make your hand [as] chained to your neck or extend it completely and [thereby] become blamed and insolvent.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids both miserliness (a hand chained to the neck) and giving everything away (a hand fully outstretched) that leaves one destitute.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s path of giving by measure, which preserves one’s wealth while still distributing it.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: measured giving that avoids both stinginess and insolvency.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which he hath given thee.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah ties the festival offering to each person’s actual means.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes one’s own measure the standard for giving.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on giving according to ability. It lacks the Kural’s explicit concern with preserving wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha advises the young householder Sigāla to divide his earnings into four parts: one for his own use and the support of others, two for investment in his work, and the fourth set aside against misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics sets a budget in which spending and giving are measured shares of income, not unlimited outflows.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s way of giving while preserving wealth: distribution fitted to one’s measure.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the budgeting logic. The fourfold division is about household economy generally rather than giving specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon welcome disguised Zeus and Hermes with what little they have: cabbage, a bit of smoked pork, simple wine. They give generously within their means and even try to kill their one goose for the guests.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their hospitality is generous yet in proportion to their modest household, and the gods reward it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates giving from one’s real measure, as the Kural advises.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative only. The myth celebrates hospitality and piety and does not explicitly teach measured giving.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “liberality resides not in the multitude of the gifts but in the state of character of the giver, and this is relative to the giver’s substance.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines liberality as giving the right amounts to the right people, relative to one’s resources. He adds that the liberal person does not neglect his own property, since he wants to be able to keep helping others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s doctrine in philosophical terms: generosity measured against one’s means, so that giving and preserving go together.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1, 1120b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on giving relative to one’s substance.

kurals.tamil:
ஆகாறு அளவிட்டி தாயினுங் கேடில்லை
போகாறு அகலாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aagaaru alavittidhu aayinum kedillai
Pogaaru agalaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: Even if the channel through which income flows in is narrow, there is no harm, as long as the channel through which it flows out is not wider.
kurals.elementary: It’s OK if you don’t earn much. What matters is that you don’t spend more than you earn. A small income with even smaller spending keeps you safe.
kurals.university: Aagaaru (the way wealth comes in) and pogaaru (the way it goes out) are channel metaphors, like the irrigation channels that feed and drain a village tank. Valluvar makes a ratio, not an absolute amount, the test of financial health. A narrow inflow (alavu ittidhu, ‘small in measure’) does no harm provided the outflow does not grow broader (agalaak kadai). The verse is often compared to Mr Micawber’s famous rule in Dickens, but it is well over a thousand years older. Within the chapter, it applies ‘knowledge of power’ to the household: one’s economic strength is the relation between inflow and outflow, not the size of either.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Arthaśāstra has the Collector-General keep accounts under separate heads: receipts (āya), expenditure (vyaya) and net balance (nīvī). The state’s strength is judged by keeping expenditure within revenue.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya institutionalises the comparison of income with outgoings as the basis of a sound treasury.
hinduism.tie_back: Āya and vyaya correspond to the Kural’s aagaaru and pogaaru, and the aim in both is that outflow should not exceed inflow.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book II, Chapter 6 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match in state accounting. Kautilya’s concern is fiscal administration, not personal contentment. Paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches contentment with modest provision rather than an endless pursuit of more.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a small income sufficient as long as needs and spending stay within it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial. It shares the idea that little is enough but has no income-and-outflow reasoning.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [they are] those who, when they spend, do so not excessively or sparingly but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the servants of the Merciful as spending in balance, neither extravagantly nor miserly.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s demand that outflow be kept in proportion to means.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on balanced spending. It does not state the income-to-expense ratio explicitly.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma teaches in the Mishnah: Who is rich? The one who rejoices in his portion.
judaism.explanation: Wealth is redefined as contentment with what one has rather than the size of one’s holdings.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that a small income need not mean harm or poverty if desire and spending stay within it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that sufficiency is relative. It lacks the Kural’s explicit comparison of income and outflow. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the householder Dīghajāṇu that balanced livelihood means knowing one’s income and expenditure and living neither too extravagantly nor too meanly, so that income exceeds expenditure. He compares this to a goldsmith holding up a scale who knows exactly how far it dips or rises.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics explicitly makes the balance of inflow against outflow a condition of welfare.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural: no harm from small income while outgoings stay smaller.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the same income-expenditure calculus with a balance-scale image. Paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises his brother Perses on household thrift: be sparing in the middle of the jar, since saving at the dregs comes too late, and observe due measure, because proportion is best in everything.
greek_mythology.explanation: The archaic Greek farmer-poet makes measured use of stores the basis of a household that lasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s rule that outflow must be kept within what comes in.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 368–369, 694 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Didactic poetry rather than myth. It shares household moderation but not the explicit income-outflow ratio. Paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.”
philosophy.explanation: Mr Micawber, himself chronically in debt, gives young David the famous rule that happiness depends not on the size of income but on whether spending stays below it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aagaaru/pogaaru ratio almost word for word.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one. Note that this is moral literature rather than formal philosophy.

kurals.tamil:
அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் வாழ்க்கை உளபோல
இல்லாகித் தோன்றாக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Alavarindhu vaazhaadhaan vaazhkkai ulapola
Illaagith thondraak kedum.
kurals.meaning: The life of one who does not live within the measure of his means will seem to prosper, then vanish without a trace.
kurals.elementary: Someone who spends as if they have more than they do might look rich for a while. But soon it all disappears, as if it had never been there.
kurals.university: The couplet diagnoses an illusion. Ula pola means ‘as if existing’: the spendthrift’s life looks abundant, but it illaagi (becomes nothing) and thondraak kedum (perishes without a trace, not even appearing afterwards). The phrase alavu arindhu vaazhaadhaan ties personal finance back to the chapter’s thesis: living well requires knowledge of one’s measure just as war does. The warning is less about spending itself than about the gap between appearance and substance. Wealth that is not measured is only apparent.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the dice game, Yudhiṣṭhira keeps staking beyond what he can afford to lose: his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadī. An emperor who has just performed the Rājasūya sacrifice ends the day with nothing.
hinduism.explanation: Yudhiṣṭhira’s vast apparent prosperity vanishes in one sitting because he does not stop within the measure of what he can afford.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s ula pola illaagi: a life that seemed full becomes empty.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva (Dyūta sub-parva; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel of unmeasured outflow wiping out apparent wealth. Gambling and fate complicate the lesson.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son takes his inheritance, lives as if it were endless, and is soon reduced to feeding pigs.
christianity.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that a life not lived within its measure looks rich and then vanishes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close narrative match. The parable’s main theme is repentance and the father’s forgiveness.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and do not spend wastefully. Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been to his Lord ungrateful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids squandering (tabdhīr) and ranks it as a serious moral failing.
islam.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s condemnation of living beyond one’s measure. The Qur’an stresses the moral gravity, while the Kural stresses the practical collapse.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the condemnation of waste. It does not describe the illusion of prosperity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.”
judaism.explanation: The wise man’s house keeps its stores, while the fool consumes everything.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s contrast between living by measure and wasting until nothing remains.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on wise conservation against foolish consumption.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists six channels through which a householder’s wealth drains away: intoxicants, roaming the streets at unseemly hours, frequenting fairs and shows, gambling, bad companions and idleness. Each is described as dissipating what has been earned.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics shows how unmeasured habits quietly empty a household.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s picture of a life that seems prosperous while its substance is draining away.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on the mechanisms of dissipation. It does not dwell on the illusion of prosperity. Paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cursed by Ceres with insatiable Hunger, King Erysichthon eats through his whole fortune. He sells his daughter Mestra again and again to buy more food, and finally, with nothing left, devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Consumption without any measure destroys first a rich king’s wealth and then the king himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is an extreme image of the Kural’s life that becomes nothing through consumption without measure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image of unmeasured consumption ending in annihilation. The cause is divine punishment for sacrilege, not ordinary imprudence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the prodigal as someone ruined through his own fault, since wasting one’s substance is a kind of ruining oneself, because life depends on property. He adds that prodigals soon exhaust their means and so are driven to take from wrong sources.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats prodigality as a vice of excess that destroys its possessor’s livelihood.
philosophy.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s claim that one who does not live within his measure is ruined, and by his own doing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1, 1120a–1121b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match on prodigality as self-ruin. Paraphrased from Ross.

kurals.tamil:
உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புர வாண்மை
வளவரை வல்லைக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu aanmai
Valavarai vallaik kedum.
kurals.meaning: Generosity that does not weigh the limits of one’s own resources will quickly exhaust one’s wealth.
kurals.elementary: Helping others is wonderful, but if you give away more than you actually have, soon you’ll have nothing left, not even enough to keep helping.
kurals.university: Oppuravu is the civic virtue of beneficence to which Valluvar devotes chapter 22 (Oppuravu Arithal), where he says that even ruin incurred through beneficence is worth buying by selling oneself (220). Here he adds the prudential counterweight. Ulavarai thookkaadha describes beneficence that does not weigh (thookku, the same balance-verb as in 471) the extent of what one has, and it rapidly (vallai) destroys the limits of one’s wealth (valavarai). The chapter thus ends where it began, with weighing. Even virtue has to be measured against capacity if it is to last.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karṇa, famous for never refusing a request, is approached by Indra disguised as a brahmin, who asks for his natural armour and earrings. Although his father Sūrya has warned him that they make him invulnerable, Karṇa cuts them from his body and gives them away. This leaves him exposed in the war that follows.
hinduism.explanation: Karṇa’s generosity ignores what he himself needs to survive and contributes to his eventual defeat.
hinduism.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning about beneficence that does not weigh one’s own limits. The epic, however, honours Karṇa’s gift as noble.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Vana Parva (Kuṇḍalāharaṇa sub-parva; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear case of generosity beyond one’s own limits leading to ruin. The Mahābhārata presents it admiringly, while Valluvar treats such giving as imprudent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that duties to one’s own household come first and may not be sacrificed.
christianity.tie_back: It supports the Kural’s limit on beneficence: generosity that ignores one’s own resources and dependents is a failure. Elsewhere, though, the gospels praise the widow who gave all she had (Mark 12:41–44).
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial. It limits generosity by household duty but is not directly about giving beyond means. There is a real tension with Mark 12.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘The excess [beyond needs].’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an answers the question of how much to give by pointing to what is surplus to one’s needs.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ulavarai thookku, weighing what one has before giving.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match: charity measured from surplus rather than at the cost of one’s own needs.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who scatters should not scatter more than one-fifth, lest he render himself destitute and need the help of other people.”
judaism.explanation: The rabbis at Usha set an upper limit on charitable giving so that the giver does not become poor himself.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s principle as a rule: beneficence that does not weigh one’s means ends in destitution.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a cap on giving to prevent self-ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Vessantara, perfecting generosity, gives away his kingdom’s auspicious rain-bringing white elephant, which leads to his exile. He then gives away his chariot, his children and even his wife.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka presents boundless giving as the Bodhisatta’s perfection (dāna-pāramī), even though it brings exile and loss.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a deliberate counterpoint to the Kural. Vessantara’s giving takes no account of his resources and ruins his estate, which is exactly what Valluvar warns against in a householder, while the Buddhist story praises it as a spiritual ideal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak and contrasting: the same situation with the opposite evaluation. It is included as the most relevant Buddhist treatment of giving beyond means. The Dīghajāṇu Sutta (AN 8.54) would give the prudential side.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Timon of Athens pours out his fortune on friends, flatterers and hangers-on without counting the cost. When his wealth is gone, those he helped abandon him, and he withdraws in bitterness to live as a labourer outside the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Timon’s generosity, which never weighed his means, destroys his wealth and leaves him friendless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a close illustration of the Kural: oppuravu that does not weigh one’s limits ruins one’s wealth quickly.
greek_mythology.source: Lucian, Timon the Misanthrope (tr. H. W. and F. G. Fowler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one narrative match. Timon is a legendary Athenian figure rather than a mythological one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero lists cautions for acts of kindness: they must not harm the recipient or others, must not exceed our means, and must suit the recipient’s worth. He argues that those who want to be more open-handed than their circumstances allow wrong their own next of kin, and are often tempted into taking wrongly from others to fund their generosity.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero makes the limit of one’s means a strict condition of true liberality.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu: beneficence that ignores one’s means is self-destructive and ends up being unjust.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.42–44 (tr. Walter Miller)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one doctrinal match. Paraphrased from the Loeb translation.
